messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun was 22, single, and worked as a UX designer in a glass-walled office downtown, where most days meant long stretches at his laptop, headphones on, neck bent toward wireframes and user flows. The hurricane had struck his coastal hometown the year before, late at night, after the power had already gone out. He had been sheltering with his family in a cramped interior hallway when the wind began to roar like something alive, and water forced itself under the doors in a cold brown sheet. By morning, the house smelled of mud, salt, and gas, and he remembered wading through debris with his neck strained upward, trying to keep his breathing steady while carrying what he could. Since then, any tightening in his neck could pull him back with startling force. When the pain flared after hours at work, or when he felt vaguely unwell and shaky in the middle of the day, the sensation did not stay ordinary for long; it slipped into the disaster memory, and suddenly he could taste the brackish, metallic flavor he associated with that night, as if it were in his mouth again. Sometimes, before any picture came, he was hit by the full heaviness of panic and dread from the storm, a raw emotional surge without a clear image, and it left him stunned at his desk.

As those episodes repeated, Arjun came to dread what they seemed to mean about people around him. He had been helping neighbors before the water rose, and he still remembered how quickly some of them had disappeared once evacuation became urgent, leaving doors open and promises unfinished. In his mind, that night had shown him that people were not what they seemed, and that sense of betrayal colored almost everything afterward. When a coworker spoke warmly about “team trust” in a meeting, Arjun found himself watching for the slight shift in tone, the hidden exit, the moment a person might turn and leave him to handle things alone. He felt isolated and set apart from his roommates, from his colleagues, even from other young men in the city who seemed to move through life without constantly measuring danger in every exchange. More and more, he believed he no longer belonged anywhere, because home had become a place that could vanish and other people could not be counted on to keep it intact.

Those beliefs made the memory itself harder to hold as a simple past event. The flood now felt so extreme and unreal that he sometimes had to stop and remind himself it had happened to him at all, as if he had watched it in a film rather than lived through it. Yet the strangeness of that disbelief did not quiet him; it made him monitor his body and surroundings even more closely, waiting for the next sign. A sore neck after a day hunched over design software, the brief wave of nausea when he skipped lunch, the smell of damp concrete in the office stairwell, or a news alert about storms on his phone could all become potent reminders. And once those reminders arrived, they did not just summon the memory; they confirmed his suspicion that something in the world was always preparing to break. He had become wary of strangers and cautious even with familiar people, assuming there was more hidden under the surface than they showed. That suspicion fed the next wave of alarm, because if people could not be trusted, then any ordinary interaction—a colleague offering help, a friend asking why he was quiet—could feel like the start of another abandonment.

Over months, Arjun began arranging his life to avoid whatever might bring that sequence back. In the office he adjusted his chair again and again to keep pressure off his neck, and when the sensation persisted he would invent reasons to step outside, gulping air on the sidewalk until the taste in his mouth faded. He kept to himself at lunch, telling others he was busy with deadlines, and he declined invitations that required travel or even weather-related planning. The more he withdrew, the more detached he felt, and the more certain he became that he was on the outside of things looking in. What brought him to treatment was that the loop was tightening: an ordinary neck ache could now derail an entire afternoon, leave him tasting the floodwater again, and drive him back into the conviction that he had been left behind in a world where no one could truly be trusted. He sought help because he was frightened that he was becoming permanently cut off from other people, and because part of him still hoped that if he could understand why his body kept dragging him back there, he might find a way to belong somewhere again.
